slides.title: Why serving is its own engineering discipline
slides.body:
Training optimizes for one number: final loss after N tokens of compute. Inference optimizes for several:

- **Latency** — time from request to response, especially TTFT (time-to-first-token).
- **Throughput** — total tokens served per second across all users.
- **Cost** — dollars per million output tokens.
- **Concurrency** — how many users can hit the same model simultaneously.

These are in tension. A naive serving stack — load the model, take requests one at a time, generate token-by-token — gets terrible throughput. A 7B model on an H100 might serve 30 tokens/sec to one user, ~30 tokens/sec to 10 users (still single-stream, queue them up), ~30 tokens/sec to 100 users (now they're waiting in line for hours).

Modern serving stacks (vLLM, TGI, TensorRT-LLM) are engineered around the specific bottlenecks of LLM inference. This lesson covers the three innovations that changed the game: continuous batching, PagedAttention, and speculative decoding.

slides.title: Worked example: vLLM's PagedAttention memory savings
slides.body: Traditional attention serving: pre-allocate KV cache for max context length per request. With max context 4096 + batch 64 + 70B model: ~5 GB allocated but most requests don't reach max length, so 30-60% memory is wasted. vLLM's PagedAttention: KV cache lives in pages (like virtual memory). Allocate pages on-demand as the response grows. Result: ~2-3× more concurrent requests on the same GPU memory. Adopted by virtually every modern LLM serving stack (TGI, TensorRT-LLM, etc.).

question.question: Derive the KV cache size
question.goal: Model: $L$ layers, $H$ heads, head dim $d$. Context length $T$. KV cache size in bytes (FP16)?

steps.prompt: Per layer: K is shape $(H, T, d)$, V is shape $(H, T, d)$. Total per layer: $2 H T d$ values. Across layers: $\times L$. FP16: $\times 2$ bytes. What's the formula?
steps.reveal: $\text{KV cache} = 4 L H T d$ bytes.

steps.prompt: For 70B model: $L = 80, H = 64, d = 128, T = 4096$. Compute (round to nearest GB).
steps.reveal: $4 \cdot 80 \cdot 64 \cdot 4096 \cdot 128 \approx 1.07 \times 10^{10}$ bytes $\approx 10.7$ GB per sequence. With batch 32: 343 GB — needs sharding.

question.finalResult: $$\boxed{\text{KV cache} = 4 L H T d \text{ bytes (FP16)}}$$ The dominant memory cost at long contexts. GQA (Grouped Query Attention) reduces $H$ effectively to $H_\text{kv}$ groups (usually 8); MQA collapses further to $H_\text{kv} = 1$. PagedAttention reduces *wasted* allocation.

slides.title: Static batching is the wrong primitive
slides.body:
Vanilla framework serving: collect K requests, batch them, run forward, return results. Two problems:

**Heterogeneous lengths.** Request A wants 50 output tokens; request B wants 500. Static batching either (a) waits for the slowest request before starting the next batch, wasting compute on completed sequences, or (b) ends every request at the shortest length, throwing away usable output.

**Long tail.** Some requests (RAG with long context, code completion with reasoning) take 10× longer than median. Static batching at K=8 with one long-tail request waits 10× as long for the entire batch.

**Continuous batching** (Yu et al. 2022, popularized by vLLM): treat the running batch as a fluid pool. As soon as a sequence in the batch finishes (hits EOS or max length), free its slot and admit a new request. Per-step throughput stays high; latency for individual requests stays low.

The practical impact: 2-5× throughput on heterogeneous workloads vs static batching. Most modern serving frameworks default to it. If your team is rolling its own inference path, this is the first optimization to add.

slides.title: PagedAttention: KV cache as virtual memory
slides.body:
The KV cache stores K and V vectors for every token in every layer. For a 7B model at seq_len 8K, that's:

```
2 (K + V) × 32 layers × 8K tokens × 32 heads × 128 head_dim × 2 bytes (fp16) ≈ 4 GB per request
```

Serving 100 concurrent requests at 8K context: 400 GB of KV cache. That doesn't fit on an 80GB H100 — even before model weights.

The naive fix: pre-allocate the maximum KV cache per request. But most requests don't use their full 8K. So static allocation is hugely wasteful — typical utilization in production is <30%.

**PagedAttention** (Kwon et al. 2023, vLLM): treat the KV cache like virtual memory. Allocate it in fixed-size *pages* (16 or 32 tokens each). Maintain a per-request page table. As a request grows, new pages get allocated on-demand from a global pool. As a request finishes, its pages return to the pool.

Result: KV cache utilization in production goes from ~30% to ~95%+. The same hardware serves 4-5× more concurrent requests. Plus a side benefit: shared prefix caching (multiple requests with the same system prompt share their KV cache pages — common for chat assistants with the same instructions).

question.question: Continuous batching gives a serving system 3× higher throughput than static batching on a heterogeneous workload. Why doesn't training use the same approach?
options: Continuous batching is too slow for training

Training batches are homogeneous (every example contributes to one gradient update; you wait for all of them anyway). The wins from continuous batching come from the heterogeneity of inference — different requests want different output lengths and arrive at different times. Training doesn't have either property
question.explanation: Training is synchronous over fixed-size batches because every gradient computation contributes to one optimizer step. Inference is per-request — each request has independent latency requirements + different output lengths + arrives independently. Continuous batching exploits exactly that asynchrony. Training analogs (ZeRO, gradient accumulation) target different problems. This is why serving-stack engineering is genuinely different from training-stack engineering.

slides.title: Speculative decoding
slides.body:
Inference is bottlenecked on memory bandwidth, not compute. Loading the 7B-parameter weights from HBM to compute one forward pass takes ~10-20 ms; the matmul itself is much faster.

**Speculative decoding** (Leviathan et al. 2022, Chen et al. 2023): use a small fast "draft" model to propose K tokens, then verify all K in parallel with the big model. The big model runs `K` candidates simultaneously, accepts as many as match its own distribution, and rolls back the rest.

The math: if the draft model agrees with the big model on `α · K` tokens on average, you get an `α · K + 1`-tokens-per-step speedup at the cost of one extra forward pass per K. With well-trained draft models (often a smaller version of the same family), `α ~ 0.7-0.9` is realistic. **Net throughput: 2-3× without any quality loss** (the key trick is the rejection sampling that makes the output indistinguishable from sampling the big model directly).

Variants: Medusa (multiple heads on the same model predict K tokens at once), EAGLE (lightweight draft network), Lookahead (no draft model — uses n-gram patterns from the running context).

When it works well: low temperature, deterministic decoding, repetitive content (code, formal text). When it doesn't: high temperature creative writing where draft and big model diverge fast.

slides.title: The serving stack — putting it together
slides.body:
A modern production serving stack composes:

1. **vLLM** (or TGI, TensorRT-LLM) for the inference engine: continuous batching + PagedAttention + speculative decoding.
2. **Tensor parallelism** within a host for low TTFT on a single request (split the matmuls 8-way; first token returns 8× faster).
3. **Quantization** (INT8 weights via SmoothQuant, INT4 via AWQ/GPTQ) to fit bigger models per GPU and reduce memory bandwidth.
4. **A request router** in front (often a thin Python service) for auth, rate limiting, prompt sanitization, output filtering.
5. **A monitoring layer** (next lesson) tracking latency, throughput, error rate per route.

The right setup depends on workload:
- **Latency-sensitive** (chat, copilot): TP=8 within host, low concurrency, speculative decoding mandatory.
- **Throughput-sensitive** (batch eval, async generation): big batch size, no speculative, possibly multi-host with request sharding.
- **Cost-sensitive** (background jobs, fine-tuning data generation): cheaper hardware (A10G, L40S), aggressive quantization, accept higher latency.

The wrong setup gets 10× the cost or 10× the latency. Right setup gets you to the throughput-cost frontier.

question.question: Why does PagedAttention specifically improve KV cache utilization (vs the naive 'pre-allocate max sequence length' approach)?
options: PagedAttention treats the KV cache like OS virtual memory: allocate fixed-size pages on demand as a sequence grows, return them when the sequence finishes. The total free pool is shared across all concurrent requests. Naive pre-allocation reserves max-length space per request even when most requests don't use it; the unused space is wasted
question.explanation: The OS analogy is exact: virtual memory + paging vs static allocation. With pages, the system multiplexes requests onto a shared physical pool, achieving high utilization regardless of variable per-request usage. Static allocation has to reserve max-length per request because reallocation mid-sequence is expensive — but max-length is rarely the actual length. PagedAttention's value is that it makes the per-token allocation cheap enough to do on demand.

slides.title: What's next
slides.body:
Inference serving is half the production story. The other half is monitoring — making sure the serving stack stays healthy + the model stays accurate as data drifts.

Next: [[monitoring-observability]] — drift, online evaluation, latency SLOs.

Key takeaways:
- Inference is memory-bandwidth-bound; throughput optimizations target memory traffic, not compute
- Continuous batching: pool requests, free slots as they finish; 2-5× throughput on heterogeneous workloads
- PagedAttention: KV cache as virtual memory; 4-5× more concurrent requests at the same hardware
- Speculative decoding: draft model proposes, big model verifies; 2-3× throughput at zero quality cost
- Real serving stacks compose all three with TP, quantization, and a monitoring layer

slides.title: Why LLM serving is its own beast
slides.body:
Two phases per request:

- **Prefill**: process the entire prompt in one big GEMM. Compute-bound; fast per token because every token in the prompt is computed in parallel.
- **Decode**: generate one token at a time, each requiring a small matmul against the KV cache. Memory-bound; the bottleneck is HBM bandwidth.

Per-step throughput is dominated by decode for any non-trivial generation length. The traditional ML-systems answer — batch many requests together — runs into a problem: requests arrive with different prompt lengths and want different generation lengths, so a fixed batch matrix is mostly padding.

**Continuous batching** schedules at the token level, mixing requests of different ages in the same forward pass. **PagedAttention** (vLLM) treats the KV cache like virtual memory, with per-request page tables — eliminating the contiguity requirement that made batching wasteful.

question.question: Your serving system uses static batching with batch size 32. Profile shows GPU utilization at ~28%. Most requests are short (~50 tokens) but a few are very long (~2k tokens). What's the cleanest fix?
options: Switch to continuous batching at the token level (e.g., vLLM-style scheduling).
question.explanation: Static batching pads every request to the longest in the batch — so 32 50-token requests waste compute padding to ~2k tokens. Continuous batching gives every token its own slot and joins requests at the token boundary, eliminating the padding waste. The other options paper over the symptom.

hints: What's being wasted in the static-batch case?
Which optimization specifically addresses heterogeneous-length requests?
slides.workedSolution: The wasted compute is padding: a static batch must pad every request to the longest length in the batch, so most slots run empty multiply-accumulates. Continuous batching schedules at the token level so each forward step processes one token per active request — no padding, no idle slots, and new requests can join mid-flight.

question.prompt: Your model server's p50 latency is fine (~120ms) but p99 spikes to 4s. Median tokens generated is 50, but a long tail of requests generate 4k+. Which serving optimization most directly addresses the p99 problem without hurting p50?
Explain in two sentences why prefill and decode benefit from different optimizations even though they're the same model.
question.rubric: Mentions that prefill is compute-bound (parallel over prompt tokens) and decode is memory-bound (sequential, KV cache reads dominate); each phase needs different batching / kernel choices.
